sections.h2: Anderson County housing and lake market
sections.html:
Anderson County hugs the Georgia line in South Carolina's northwest and belongs to the Greenville-Anderson-Greer metro. Anderson, the city, is the county seat. At the 2020 count there were 80,372 households among 89,123 housing units, with 9.8% of the units empty, and owners lived in 73.2% of homes that were occupied. By 2025 the population estimate had reached 219,930.

Part of Lake Hartwell, a 55,950-acre Army Corps of Engineers reservoir with close to 1,000 miles of shoreline, falls inside the county. Waterfront buyers are not the people shopping a mill-town house in Pelzer or a newer place near Powdersville. Five school districts, numbered 1 through 5, cover the county, and the street decides which one applies, so request a boundary lookup from the districts before you list.

The county accepts payment from September 30 until January 15. Then penalties begin. First comes 3%, charged January 16 or 30 days after mailing if that is later. February 2 brings another 7%, and March 17 another 5%, when an execution may be issued.

Anderson County property tax rules at a glance
TopicRule
Who collectsCounty treasurer, under Department of Revenue supervision
Payment windowSeptember 30 to January 15
Late penalties3%, then 7%, then 5%
Mailed paymentsThe U.S. postmark controls
Objection to assessmentWithin 90 days of the notice mailing

For payment options and your parcel's current balance, phone the Anderson County Treasurer.

sections.h2: What a reassessment notice tells you
sections.html:
A value increase of $1,000 or more, or a parcel's first assessment, obliges the assessor to send you a notice. Expect to see market value, assessment ratio, acreage or lots, tax map number and appeal instructions on it.

You get 90 days from mailing to object in writing. When the entire county is reassessed, almost every notice must be mailed by October 1, and if that does not happen, the prior year's assessment stands for the current tax year.

  • Hold on to the notice, because your deadline counts from its mailing day.
  • State which value or ratio you dispute.
  • No notice this year? You can still appeal, in writing, whenever you like.
  • An appeal filed ahead of the first penalty date counts toward that tax year.

Ask the Anderson County Assessor for the right form and the filing address.

sections.h2: Your mailing address after a sale
sections.html:
Picture a bill mailed to the previous owner after title moved mid-year. When the new owner received nothing in time, the treasurer shall waive the penalty, as S.C. Code 12-45-180(B) provides.

A waiver is not guaranteed, though. Envelopes addressed to a late parent or a past owner can sit unopened while the penalty dates roll by. The deed holder should phone both offices to verify the address and ask for the balance in writing.

  • Tell the treasurer where to mail the bill as soon as the deed is recorded.
  • Have the unpaid balance and penalty dates put on paper.
  • Keep the closing statement with your payment receipts.

sections.h2: Selling a house that owes tax
sections.html:
Back tax will not stop you from selling. The Treasurer can quote a payoff, with a date through which it holds, and your title company handles the rest. The open tax comes out of your proceeds at closing, and the buyer receives the house without a tax cloud.

Because penalties rise on fixed dates, a payoff expires. Ask what the number becomes if closing slips. For a house that came through an estate, learn where the notices have been going, since a stale address is how many heirs hear about a bill late.

Cash buyers will look at a house in any condition, older mill-era or newer subdivision. They price the house, the title and the tax status, and the payoff and recording steps are the same as in a financed sale.

Start with an inventory. Find the latest tax bill, copy down the tax map number and amount, and mark whether it is paid. Locate your assessment notice and record its mailing date, which starts the 90-day objection period. Then call the Treasurer about open years and the assessor about any notice that never arrived.

Then think about the buyer. Lakeside, rural and commuter-side parcels each draw their own people, and houses near Interstate 85 on the Greenville side suit those who work elsewhere. Disclose needed repairs early, and keep the payoff letter within reach so the title company never waits on you.

Finally, settle the address change. After closing, the buyer gives both offices a current address, and you file a copy of your own request.

sections.h2: If your tax payment is mailed
sections.html:
Sending a check near a deadline is risky. What counts is the postmark, so go to a post office counter and get a postmarked receipt rather than dropping an envelope in a box. Put the tax map number on the check and on a note inside.

Should a payment cross a penalty date in transit, bring the postmarked receipt and a copy of the check to the treasurer. Paper is what settles a timing dispute. During a pending sale, tell the title company about any payment in transit so the payoff letter shows it and nothing is paid twice.

sections.h2: Settling the tax at the closing table
sections.html:
On closing day the title company gathers the payoff letter, your closing statement and the buyer's information, and compares them. If the year's bill is open, the title company can pay it at the table, and anything left over reaches you. If it is already paid, the receipt goes in the file so the buyer sees nothing outstanding.

Bring photo identification and the tax map number, and confirm that the mailing address on file will change to the buyer's. Ask for a copy of the final statement showing the tax payment. If the figure on the payoff and the figure at the table differ, ask the title company to explain why before you sign, since a changed good-through date is the usual cause.

Afterward, keep the closing statement, the payoff letter and the tax receipt together for your own records. If a bill for a year you thought was settled ever turns up, those three papers show what was paid, when and by whom. They also help if the new owner's first notice goes astray, because you can show the treasurer the date the deed was recorded and the address you reported.

If you are selling an inherited house, also tell the title company who is signing for the estate so the paperwork matches the name on the deed. A mismatch there delays more closings than the tax bill does.

faqs.q: When are Anderson County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Payment opens September 30 and closes January 15, with penalties starting the next day or 30 days after mailing, if later.

faqs.q: What are the penalties for paying late?
faqs.a: A 3% charge, then 7% after February 1, then 5% after March 16, and finally an execution.

faqs.q: How long do I have to dispute my assessment?
faqs.a: Ninety days, counted from the mailing of the assessor's notice. Submit it in writing on the form the Anderson County Assessor supplies.

faqs.q: What if the tax bill went to the old owner?
faqs.a: The treasurer shall waive it when the notice went to the prior owner and you received none in time. Ask in writing.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Anderson County house that owes tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff, and your closing agent takes the open tax out of the proceeds.
